body.heading: The problem with perfect budgets
paragraphs: A perfect budget assumes a perfect month: no birthdays, no broken shoes, no friend visiting from out of town. The first surprise blows a hole in it, and many people abandon the whole plan because it is "already ruined."
The budget was not ruined; it was brittle. Real months wobble, so a workable budget wobbles with them.

body.heading: Build the flex in
paragraphs: Add a small "life happens" line to the budget — even $20 or $30 a month — that exists purely for surprises. In a month with no surprises, the leftover rolls into savings, which makes the flexible month feel like a win.

Also decide in advance which categories may borrow from each other. If eating out runs over, perhaps entertainment lends it the difference. Borrowing inside the plan is not cheating; it is the plan working.

body.heading: Review, adjust, continue
paragraphs: Once a month, spend ten minutes comparing the plan with what actually happened, and adjust the numbers that were plainly wrong. A budget that learns from last month gets more accurate every time you use it.

Think of the first version of any budget as a draft written in pencil. The second month is always closer to the truth, and by the third, the numbers usually look less like wishes and more like your actual life.

takeaway: Give your budget a small surprise fund and permission for categories to lend to each other, and it will bend through real months instead of snapping.
